expectedText:
EMPLOYER LIABILITY FOR WORKPLACE HARASSMENT: SUPERVISORS, COWORKERS, AND NONEMPLOYEES (GOV. CODE §§ 12940(J), 12940(K), 12923, 12926(T); STATE DEPT. OF HEALTH SERVICES V. SUPERIOR COURT) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
Acme, Inc. maintains this information sheet, provided to Jordan Lee, to describe what California law says about when an employer is legally responsible for harassment in the workplace under the Fair Employment and Housing Act. It describes the prohibition in Government Code section 12940, subdivision (j); the different standard the statute sets for harassment by a supervisor and harassment by a coworker; the employer’s separate responsibility for the acts of nonemployees; the personal liability of the individual who harasses; the statutory duty to take all reasonable steps to prevent harassment, including the separate unlawful practice defined by section 12940, subdivision (k); the statutory definition of “supervisor”; the California Supreme Court’s holding in State Dept. of Health Services v. Superior Court that an employer is strictly liable for hostile environment sexual harassment by a supervisor, and that the avoidable consequences doctrine limits the damages recoverable without excusing that liability; the court’s conclusion that the federal Ellerth/Faragher affirmative defense does not apply to the FEHA; and the Legislature’s declarations in Government Code section 12923 about the conduct standard those liability rules attach to. It describes the law; it does not evaluate any particular incident, complaint, investigation, or claim, and it does not state what any person should do.

THE STATUTORY PROHIBITION AND WHO IS COVERED BY IT
The Fair Employment and Housing Act makes workplace harassment an unlawful employment practice. Government Code section 12940, subdivision (j)(1), makes it unlawful for an employer, a labor organization, an employment agency, an apprenticeship training program or any training program leading to employment, or any other person, because of a listed protected characteristic, to harass an employee, an applicant, an unpaid intern or volunteer, or a person providing services pursuant to a contract. The listed characteristics are race, religious creed, color, national origin, ancestry, physical disability, mental disability, medical condition, genetic information, marital status, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, age, sexual orientation, reproductive health decisionmaking, and veteran or military status.

For the harassment subdivision only, the statute supplies its own definition of “employer”: any person regularly employing one or more persons, or regularly receiving the services of one or more persons providing services pursuant to a contract, or any person acting as an agent of an employer, directly or indirectly, the state, or any political or civil subdivision of the state, and cities. The statute then states that the definition of “employer” in Government Code section 12926, subdivision (d), applies to all provisions of section 12940 other than the harassment subdivision. The subdivision also states that “harassment” because of sex includes sexual harassment, gender harassment, and harassment based on pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions, and that sexually harassing conduct need not be motivated by sexual desire.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "For an employer, labor organization, employment agency, apprenticeship training program or any training program leading to employment, or any other person, because of race, religious creed, color, national origin, ancestry, physical disability, mental disability, medical condition, genetic information, marital status, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, age, sexual orientation, reproductive health decisionmaking, or veteran or military status, to harass an employee, an applicant, an unpaid intern or volunteer, or a person providing services pursuant to a contract."
  — California Government Code § 12940 (Official California Legislative Information), Gov. Code § 12940, subd. (j)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  "For purposes of this subdivision only, “employer” means any person regularly employing one or more persons or regularly receiving the services of one or more persons providing services pursuant to a contract, or any person acting as an agent of an employer, directly or indirectly, the state, or any political or civil subdivision of the state, and cities. The definition of “employer” in subdivision (d) of Section 12926 applies to all provisions of this section other than this subdivision."
  — California Government Code § 12940 (Official California Legislative Information), Gov. Code § 12940, subd. (j)(4)(A) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  "For purposes of this subdivision, “harassment” because of sex includes sexual harassment, gender harassment, and harassment based on pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions. Sexually harassing conduct need not be motivated by sexual desire."
  — California Government Code § 12940 (Official California Legislative Information), Gov. Code § 12940, subd. (j)(4)(C) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  Known gap: The one-or-more-persons definition quoted below is expressly limited to “this subdivision” — subdivision (j) of section 12940 — and the statute says so in the same paragraph; this clause does not state what employee count applies to any other subdivision, claim, or statute. Subparagraph (j)(4)(B), not quoted here, excludes certain religious associations and nonprofit religious corporations from that definition except as provided in Government Code section 12926.2, and paragraph (j)(5), not quoted here, sets out three criteria that define “a person providing services pursuant to a contract.” This clause describes the prohibition itself; the separate question of who is answerable for a given act of harassment is addressed by the clauses that follow. Neither the statutory text quoted here nor any other source cited in this document defines what conduct amounts to harassment in a particular workplace, and no clause of this document evaluates any particular incident.

HARASSMENT BY A SUPERVISOR: STRICT LIABILITY UNDER THE FEHA
In State Dept. of Health Services v. Superior Court (2003) 31 Cal.4th 1026, the California Supreme Court decided whether, under the FEHA, an employer is strictly liable for hostile environment sexual harassment by a supervisor, and whether the damages recoverable from the employer include damages the plaintiff could have avoided by reporting the harassment. The court concluded that an employer is strictly liable under the FEHA for sexual harassment by a supervisor.

The court drew that rule from the structure of the statute rather than from agency law. Because section 12940, subdivision (j)(1), imposes a knew-or-should-have-known standard only for harassment “by an employee other than an agent or supervisor,” the court reasoned, the FEHA by implication makes the employer strictly liable for harassment by a supervisor. The court added that by choosing that phrasing the Legislature indicated that all acts of harassment by a supervisor are exempted from the negligence standard, whether or not the supervisor was then acting as the employer’s agent, and that agency principles come into play only when the harasser is not a supervisor.

A footnote to that discussion states a limit: the analysis assumes the supervisor is acting in the capacity of supervisor when the harassment occurs, and the employer is not strictly liable for a supervisor’s acts of harassment resulting from a completely private relationship unconnected with the employment and not occurring at the workplace or during normal working hours.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "At issue here is whether, under the FEHA, an employer is strictly liable for hostile environment sexual harassment by a supervisor and whether the damages a plaintiff may recover from the employer in such a case include damages that the plaintiff could have avoided by reporting incidents of harassment to the employer."
  — State Dept. of Health Services v. Superior Court (2003) 31 Cal.4th 1026 (CourtListener text), 31 Cal.4th 1026, 1034 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2520995/state-department-of-health-services-v-superior-court/)
  "We conclude that an employer is strictly liable under the FEHA for sexual harassment by a supervisor."
  — State Dept. of Health Services v. Superior Court (2003) 31 Cal.4th 1026 (CourtListener text), 31 Cal.4th 1026, 1034 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2520995/state-department-of-health-services-v-superior-court/)
  "Because the FEHA imposes this negligence standard only for harassment “by an employee other than an agent or supervisor” (§ 12940, subd. (j)(1)), by implication the FEHA makes the employer strictly liable for harassment by a supervisor."
  — State Dept. of Health Services v. Superior Court (2003) 31 Cal.4th 1026 (CourtListener text), 31 Cal.4th 1026, 1041 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2520995/state-department-of-health-services-v-superior-court/)
  "the Legislature has indicated that all acts of harassment by a supervisor are to be exempted from the negligence standard, whether or not the supervisor was then acting as the employer’s agent, and that agency principles come into play only when the harasser is not a supervisor."
  — State Dept. of Health Services v. Superior Court (2003) 31 Cal.4th 1026 (CourtListener text), 31 Cal.4th 1026, 1041 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2520995/state-department-of-health-services-v-superior-court/)
  "Of course, this analysis assumes the supervisor is acting in the capacity of supervisor when the harassment occurs. The employer is not strictly liable for a supervisor’s acts of harassment resulting from a completely private relationship unconnected with the employment and not occurring at the workplace or during normal working hours."
  — State Dept. of Health Services v. Superior Court (2003) 31 Cal.4th 1026 (CourtListener text), 31 Cal.4th 1026, fn. 3 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2520995/state-department-of-health-services-v-superior-court/)
  Known gap: The holding as the court stated it concerns hostile environment sexual harassment by a supervisor; the court’s reasoning rests on statutory language that is not limited to sex, but this document does not state how that reasoning applies to harassment based on any other protected characteristic, because the opinion decided a sexual harassment case. Strict liability here describes liability for the harassment, not the amount of damages recoverable; the damages question is addressed in later clauses. The footnote quoted below appears in the CourtListener rendering of the opinion in a block of footnotes collected after the signature line and without its footnote number, so the official-reports page on which it is printed could not be determined from the fetched text; its citation below therefore gives the footnote without a page pincite. Whether a particular individual is a supervisor, and whether particular conduct is harassment, are questions this document does not address.

HARASSMENT BY A COWORKER: THE KNEW-OR-SHOULD-HAVE-KNOWN STANDARD
The statute sets a different rule for harassment by an employee who is not an agent or supervisor. Under section 12940, subdivision (j)(1), harassment of an employee, an applicant, an unpaid intern or volunteer, or a person providing services pursuant to a contract by an employee other than an agent or supervisor is unlawful if the entity, or its agents or supervisors, knows or should have known of the conduct and fails to take immediate and appropriate corrective action.

In State Dept. of Health Services v. Superior Court, the California Supreme Court described that provision as making the employer liable for harassment by a nonsupervisory employee only if the employer knew or should have known of the harassing conduct and failed to take immediate and appropriate corrective action, and characterized it in three words: “This is a negligence standard.” That is the contrast from which the court inferred the strict liability rule for supervisors described in the preceding clause.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Harassment of an employee, an applicant, an unpaid intern or volunteer, or a person providing services pursuant to a contract by an employee, other than an agent or supervisor, shall be unlawful if the entity, or its agents or supervisors, knows or should have known of this conduct and fails to take immediate and appropriate corrective action."
  — California Government Code § 12940 (Official California Legislative Information), Gov. Code § 12940, subd. (j)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  "The employer is liable for harassment by a nonsupervisory employee only if the employer (a) knew or should have known of the harassing conduct and (b) failed to take immediate and appropriate corrective action."
  — State Dept. of Health Services v. Superior Court (2003) 31 Cal.4th 1026 (CourtListener text), 31 Cal.4th 1026, 1041 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2520995/state-department-of-health-services-v-superior-court/)
  "This is a negligence standard."
  — State Dept. of Health Services v. Superior Court (2003) 31 Cal.4th 1026 (CourtListener text), 31 Cal.4th 1026, 1041 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2520995/state-department-of-health-services-v-superior-court/)
  Known gap: The statute does not define “immediate and appropriate corrective action,” and no source cited in this document states what response satisfies that requirement in any particular case; State Dept. of Health Services described the coworker standard by way of contrast and did not decide a coworker harassment case. The statute’s phrase “other than an agent or supervisor” places an employer’s agents on the supervisor side of the line as a matter of text; this document does not state who is an agent of an employer in any particular arrangement. Whether the employer knew or should have known of particular conduct is a question of fact this document does not address.

HARASSMENT BY NONEMPLOYEES
The same subdivision reaches conduct by people who are not the employer’s employees at all. Section 12940, subdivision (j)(1), states that an employer may also be responsible for the acts of nonemployees, with respect to harassment of employees, applicants, unpaid interns or volunteers, or persons providing services pursuant to a contract in the workplace, if the employer, or its agents or supervisors, knows or should have known of the conduct and fails to take immediate and appropriate corrective action — the same knew-or-should-have-known formulation the statute uses for coworkers.

The subdivision adds a further instruction for those cases: in reviewing cases involving the acts of nonemployees, the extent of the employer’s control and any other legal responsibility that the employer may have with respect to the conduct of those nonemployees shall be considered.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "An employer may also be responsible for the acts of nonemployees, with respect to harassment of employees, applicants, unpaid interns or volunteers, or persons providing services pursuant to a contract in the workplace, if the employer, or its agents or supervisors, knows or should have known of the conduct and fails to take immediate and appropriate corrective action."
  — California Government Code § 12940 (Official California Legislative Information), Gov. Code § 12940, subd. (j)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  "In reviewing cases involving the acts of nonemployees, the extent of the employer’s control and any other legal responsibility that the employer may have with respect to the conduct of those nonemployees shall be considered."
  — California Government Code § 12940 (Official California Legislative Information), Gov. Code § 12940, subd. (j)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  Known gap: The statute says an employer “may also be responsible,” and conditions that responsibility on knowledge and on the failure to take immediate and appropriate corrective action; it does not list who counts as a nonemployee, and no source cited in this document states how the control factor is weighed in any particular case. The provision by its terms addresses harassment “in the workplace.” State Dept. of Health Services did not involve a nonemployee harasser and is not cited in this clause.

PERSONAL LIABILITY OF THE INDIVIDUAL WHO HARASSES
The statute addresses the individual harasser separately from the employer. Section 12940, subdivision (j)(3), states that an employee of an entity subject to the subdivision is personally liable for any harassment prohibited by the section that is perpetrated by that employee, regardless of whether the employer or covered entity knows or should have known of the conduct and fails to take immediate and appropriate corrective action.

That personal liability therefore does not depend on the employer’s knowledge or on the employer’s response. The subdivision also contains its own characterization of its effect: its provisions are declaratory of existing law, except for the new duties imposed on employers with regard to harassment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "An employee of an entity subject to this subdivision is personally liable for any harassment prohibited by this section that is perpetrated by the employee, regardless of whether the employer or covered entity knows or should have known of the conduct and fails to take immediate and appropriate corrective action."
  — California Government Code § 12940 (Official California Legislative Information), Gov. Code § 12940, subd. (j)(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  "The provisions of this subdivision are declaratory of existing law, except for the new duties imposed on employers with regard to harassment."
  — California Government Code § 12940 (Official California Legislative Information), Gov. Code § 12940, subd. (j)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  Known gap: Paragraph (j)(3) by its terms addresses “harassment prohibited by this section that is perpetrated by the employee”; no source cited in this document addresses personal liability of an individual for the other unlawful employment practices defined by section 12940, such as discrimination or retaliation, and this document does not state whether such liability exists. The “declaratory of existing law” sentence quoted below is the Legislature’s own statement about the subdivision; this document does not trace which sentences of the subdivision were added by which enactment, because the Legislative Counsel’s published section carries only the credit line for the most recent amendment. Whether particular conduct by a particular individual is harassment is not addressed here.

THE DUTY TO TAKE ALL REASONABLE STEPS TO PREVENT HARASSMENT
Beyond responsibility for particular acts, the FEHA imposes a preventive duty. Section 12940, subdivision (j)(1), states that an entity shall take all reasonable steps to prevent harassment from occurring, and that loss of tangible job benefits shall not be necessary in order to establish harassment.

Section 12940, subdivision (k), states a separate unlawful employment practice: for an employer, labor organization, employment agency, apprenticeship training program, or any training program leading to employment, to fail to take all reasonable steps necessary to prevent discrimination and harassment from occurring. Subdivision (k) is worded to cover both discrimination and harassment, while the sentence in subdivision (j)(1) is worded for harassment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "An entity shall take all reasonable steps to prevent harassment from occurring. Loss of tangible job benefits shall not be necessary in order to establish harassment."
  — California Government Code § 12940 (Official California Legislative Information), Gov. Code § 12940, subd. (j)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  "For an employer, labor organization, employment agency, apprenticeship training program, or any training program leading to employment, to fail to take all reasonable steps necessary to prevent discrimination and harassment from occurring."
  — California Government Code § 12940 (Official California Legislative Information), Gov. Code § 12940, subd. (k) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  Known gap: Neither provision lists the steps that count as “all reasonable steps,” and no source cited in this document states what an employer must do in any particular workplace to satisfy either provision. No source cited here addresses whether a private plaintiff may recover on a subdivision (k) claim without an underlying finding of actual discrimination or harassment; that question is not decided by State Dept. of Health Services and is not answered by the statutory text quoted below. California’s separate mandatory harassment-prevention training requirement appears in Government Code section 12950.1 and is described by a different document in this corpus; it is not quoted or summarized here.

HOW THE FEHA DEFINES “SUPERVISOR”
Because the statute divides liability along the supervisor line, the definition of “supervisor” carries the weight of that division. Government Code section 12926, subdivision (t), defines a supervisor as any individual having the authority, in the interest of the employer, to hire, transfer, suspend, lay off, recall, promote, discharge, assign, reward, or discipline other employees, or the responsibility to direct them, or to adjust their grievances, or effectively to recommend that action, if, in connection with the foregoing, the exercise of that authority is not of a merely routine or clerical nature, but requires the use of independent judgment.

The definition is phrased in the alternative: authority over the listed personnel actions, or the responsibility to direct other employees, or authority to adjust their grievances, or authority effectively to recommend those actions, each qualified by the requirement that exercising the authority take more than routine or clerical judgment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "“Supervisor” means any individual having the authority, in the interest of the employer, to hire, transfer, suspend, lay off, recall, promote, discharge, assign, reward, or discipline other employees, or the responsibility to direct them, or to adjust their grievances, or effectively to recommend that action, if, in connection with the foregoing, the exercise of that authority is not of a merely routine or clerical nature, but requires the use of independent judgment."
  — California Government Code § 12926 (Official California Legislative Information), Gov. Code § 12926, subd. (t) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12926.)
  Known gap: Section 12926 supplies definitions “as used in this part” — the FEHA — and the definition quoted below is not limited to the harassment subdivision. Job title is not part of the definition, and no source cited in this document states whether any particular position carries the authority or responsibility the definition describes; that is a factual question this document does not address. State Dept. of Health Services did not turn on the definition, because the harasser’s supervisory status was not in dispute there.

THE AVOIDABLE CONSEQUENCES DEFENSE TO DAMAGES
State Dept. of Health Services also decided a damages question. The court concluded that the avoidable consequences doctrine applies to damage claims under the FEHA, so that a plaintiff’s recoverable damages do not include damages the plaintiff could have avoided with reasonable effort and without undue risk, expense, or humiliation.

In this context the court held that the defense has three elements: the employer took reasonable steps to prevent and correct workplace sexual harassment; the employee unreasonably failed to use the preventive and corrective measures the employer provided; and reasonable use of the employer’s procedures would have prevented at least some of the harm the employee suffered. The court described the effect of the defense as allowing the employer to escape liability for those damages, and only those damages, that the employee more likely than not could have prevented with reasonable effort and without undue risk, expense, or humiliation, by taking advantage of the employer’s internal complaint procedures appropriately designed to prevent and eliminate sexual harassment. The court stated that the defendant bears the burden of pleading and proving a defense based on the avoidable consequences doctrine, and that a failure to report harassment, by itself, is insufficient to establish the defense: the employer must also show that the failure to report was unreasonable under the circumstances and that, more likely than not, using the employer-provided internal remedies would have prevented at least some of the claimed damages.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "We further conclude that the avoidable consequences doctrine applies to damage claims under the FEHA, and that under that doctrine a plaintiff’s recoverable damages do not include those damages that the plaintiff could have avoided with reasonable effort and without undue risk, expense, or humiliation."
  — State Dept. of Health Services v. Superior Court (2003) 31 Cal.4th 1026 (CourtListener text), 31 Cal.4th 1026, 1034 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2520995/state-department-of-health-services-v-superior-court/)
  "We hold, therefore, that in a FEHA action against an employer for hostile environment sexual harassment by a supervisor, an employer may plead and prove a defense based on the avoidable consequences doctrine. In this particular context, the defense has three elements: (1) the employer took reasonable steps to prevent and correct workplace sexual harassment; (2) the employee unreasonably failed to use the preventive and corrective measures that the employer provided; and (3) reasonable use of the employer’s procedures would have prevented at least some of the harm that the employee suffered."
  — State Dept. of Health Services v. Superior Court (2003) 31 Cal.4th 1026 (CourtListener text), 31 Cal.4th 1026, 1044 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2520995/state-department-of-health-services-v-superior-court/)
  "This defense will allow the employer to escape liability for those damages, and only those damages, that the employee more likely than not could have prevented with reasonable effort and without undue risk, expense, or humiliation, by taking advantage of the employer’s internal complaint procedures appropriately designed to prevent and eliminate sexual harassment."
  — State Dept. of Health Services v. Superior Court (2003) 31 Cal.4th 1026 (CourtListener text), 31 Cal.4th 1026, 1044 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2520995/state-department-of-health-services-v-superior-court/)
  "The defendant bears the burden of pleading and proving a defense based on the avoidable consequences doctrine."
  — State Dept. of Health Services v. Superior Court (2003) 31 Cal.4th 1026 (CourtListener text), 31 Cal.4th 1026, 1044 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2520995/state-department-of-health-services-v-superior-court/)
  "as we have explained, an employee’s failure to report a supervisor’s harassment to management, by itself, is insufficient to establish an avoidable consequences defense. To establish the defense, the employer must also show that the employee’s failure to report the harassment was unreasonable under the circumstances and that, more likely than not, using the employer-provided internal remedies would have prevented at least some of the employee’s claimed damages from occurring."
  — State Dept. of Health Services v. Superior Court (2003) 31 Cal.4th 1026 (CourtListener text), 31 Cal.4th 1026, 1046 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2520995/state-department-of-health-services-v-superior-court/)
  Known gap: The holding is framed for a FEHA action against an employer for hostile environment sexual harassment by a supervisor; this document does not state how the doctrine applies to other FEHA claims. The elements as the court stated them turn on facts — what steps the employer took, what procedures existed, whether the employee’s conduct was unreasonable in the particular employment setting, and what harm reasonable use of those procedures would have prevented — and no clause of this document evaluates any of them for any situation. The court also observed that deciding when a harassed employee first suffered compensable harm and when a reasonable employee would have reported the harassment will in many instances present disputed factual issues; that observation is described, not quoted, in this clause. Nothing here states what any employee or employer should do about reporting.

THE DEFENSE AFFECTS DAMAGES, NOT LIABILITY
The court was explicit that the avoidable consequences defense does not undo the employer’s liability. It emphasized that the defense affects damages, not liability, and that an employer that has exercised reasonable care nonetheless remains strictly liable for harm a sexually harassed employee could not have avoided through reasonable care.

The court described the division in time: if the employer establishes that the employee, by taking reasonable steps to use employer-provided complaint procedures, could have caused the harassing conduct to cease, the employer nonetheless remains liable for any compensable harm the employee suffered before the time at which the harassment would have ceased, and avoids liability only for the harm incurred after that point. In its concluding section the court restated the limits of the holding: an employer continues to be strictly liable for hostile environment sexual harassment by a supervisor, and an employee’s failure to report harassment to the employer is not a defense on the merits but at most serves to reduce the damages recoverable.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "We emphasize that the defense affects damages, not liability. An employer that has exercised reasonable care nonetheless remains strictly liable for harm a sexually harassed employee could not have avoided through reasonable care."
  — State Dept. of Health Services v. Superior Court (2003) 31 Cal.4th 1026 (CourtListener text), 31 Cal.4th 1026, 1045 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2520995/state-department-of-health-services-v-superior-court/)
  "If the employer establishes that the employee, by taking reasonable steps to utilize employer-provided complaint procedures, could have caused the harassing conduct to cease, the employer will nonetheless remain liable for any compensable harm the employee suffered before the time at which the harassment would have ceased, and the employer avoids liability only for the harm the employee incurred thereafter."
  — State Dept. of Health Services v. Superior Court (2003) 31 Cal.4th 1026 (CourtListener text), 31 Cal.4th 1026, 1045 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2520995/state-department-of-health-services-v-superior-court/)
  "We reiterate the limits of our holding. An employer continues to be strictly liable for hostile environment sexual harassment by a supervisor. An employee’s failure to report harassment to the employer is not a defense on the merits to the employee’s action under the FEHA, but at most it serves to reduce the damages recoverable."
  — State Dept. of Health Services v. Superior Court (2003) 31 Cal.4th 1026 (CourtListener text), 31 Cal.4th 1026, 1049 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2520995/state-department-of-health-services-v-superior-court/)
  Known gap: Whether the defense is partial or complete in a given case, and whether any particular evidentiary showing establishes it, are questions the court described as predominately factual and on which it expressly ventured no opinion; this document does not address them either. The passages quoted below concern the avoidable consequences doctrine as applied to FEHA hostile environment sexual harassment by a supervisor and say nothing about any other defense, about statutory deadlines for bringing a claim, or about remedies other than damages.

WHY THE FEDERAL ELLERTH/FARAGHER DEFENSE DOES NOT APPLY
The employer in State Dept. of Health Services argued that the employee’s failure to use its internal procedures was a complete defense, relying on the United States Supreme Court’s decisions in Burlington Industries, Inc. v. Ellerth and Faragher v. City of Boca Raton. Under those decisions, in a Title VII action for workplace sexual harassment not involving a tangible employment action, an employer may establish a partial or complete defense by proving that it exercised reasonable care to prevent and correct promptly any sexually harassing behavior and that the plaintiff employee unreasonably failed to take advantage of any preventive or corrective opportunities provided by the employer or to avoid harm otherwise.

The California Supreme Court did not import that defense into the FEHA. It reasoned that the federal defense rests in part on agency principles, while the FEHA’s text removes supervisor harassment from the negligence standard regardless of agency; to the extent the federal defense was derived from agency principles, the court held, its reasoning is not applicable to the FEHA. What the court did take from the federal cases was the separate, damages-based avoidable consequences doctrine described in the preceding clauses.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "an employer may establish a partial or complete defense by proving: “(a) that the employer exercised reasonable care to prevent and correct promptly any sexually harassing behavior, and (b) that the plaintiff employee unreasonably failed to take advantage of any preventive or corrective opportunities provided by the employer or to avoid harm otherwise.”"
  — State Dept. of Health Services v. Superior Court (2003) 31 Cal.4th 1026 (CourtListener text), 31 Cal.4th 1026, 1036 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2520995/state-department-of-health-services-v-superior-court/)
  "To the extent the United States Supreme Court derived the Ellerth/Faragher defense from agency principles, therefore, its reasoning is not applicable to the FEHA."
  — State Dept. of Health Services v. Superior Court (2003) 31 Cal.4th 1026 (CourtListener text), 31 Cal.4th 1026, 1041 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2520995/state-department-of-health-services-v-superior-court/)
  Known gap: This clause describes the federal defense only as the California Supreme Court described it in 2003 in the course of declining to apply it; the federal authorities themselves were not fetched for this document, and nothing here states the current content of federal law or how Title VII claims are decided. The quotation of the federal standard below is the California court’s quotation of Ellerth and Faragher, reproduced as it appears in the fetched California opinion.

THE CONDUCT STANDARD THE LIABILITY RULES ATTACH TO
The liability rules described above attach to conduct that qualifies as harassment. In Government Code section 12923 the Legislature declared its intent with regard to application of the laws about harassment contained in the FEHA. Section 12923, subdivision (a), declares that harassment creates a hostile, offensive, oppressive, or intimidating work environment and deprives victims of their statutory right to work in a place free of discrimination when the harassing conduct sufficiently offends, humiliates, distresses, or intrudes upon its victim, so as to disrupt the victim’s emotional tranquility in the workplace, affect the victim’s ability to perform the job as usual, or otherwise interfere with and undermine the victim’s personal sense of well-being.

Subdivision (b) states that a single incident of harassing conduct is sufficient to create a triable issue regarding the existence of a hostile work environment if the harassing conduct has unreasonably interfered with the plaintiff’s work performance or created an intimidating, hostile, or offensive working environment. Subdivision (e) states that harassment cases are rarely appropriate for disposition on summary judgment. In Government Code section 12923 the Legislature declared its intent with regard to application of the laws about harassment contained in the FEHA. Section 12923, subdivision (a), declares that harassment creates a hostile, offensive, oppressive, or intimidating work environment and deprives victims of their statutory right to work in a place free of discrimination when the harassing conduct sufficiently offends, humiliates, distresses, or intrudes upon its victim, so as to disrupt the victim’s emotional tranquility in the workplace, affect the victim’s ability to perform the job as usual, or otherwise interfere with and undermine the victim’s personal sense of well-being.

Subdivision (b) states that a single incident of harassing conduct is sufficient to create a triable issue regarding the existence of a hostile work environment if the harassing conduct has unreasonably interfered with the plaintiff’s work performance or created an intimidating, hostile, or offensive working environment. Subdivision (e) states that harassment cases are rarely appropriate for disposition on summary judgment. Section 12940, subdivision (j)(1), separately provides that loss of tangible job benefits shall not be necessary in order to establish harassment.

The authorities described here are bounded in ways that appear on their face. Section 12940, subdivision (j), addresses harassment; the other subdivisions of section 12940 address other unlawful employment practices, including discrimination and retaliation, and are not described here. The one-or-more-persons definition of “employer” applies to the harassment subdivision only, and the statute says so expressly. State Dept. of Health Services decided a case about hostile environment sexual harassment by a supervisor and addressed employer liability and the measure of damages; it did not decide what conduct is harassment, who is a supervisor, or how a coworker harassment case is to be resolved.

This document does not describe the procedures for filing a complaint with the Civil Rights Department or in court, the deadlines that apply to such a complaint, the remedies available, attorney’s fees, or the employer’s obligations under the mandatory harassment-prevention training statute, Government Code section 12950.1, which a separate document in this corpus describes. It does not describe federal law under Title VII beyond the California Supreme Court’s account of the Ellerth and Faragher defense, and it does not describe any local ordinance, collective bargaining agreement, or employer policy.

citations.case: California Government Code § 12940 (Official California Legislative Information)
citations.quote: Harassment of an employee, an applicant, an unpaid intern or volunteer, or a person providing services pursuant to a contract by an employee, other than an agent or supervisor, shall be unlawful if the entity, or its agents or supervisors, knows or should have known of this conduct and fails to take immediate and appropriate corrective action.

citations.case: State Dept. of Health Services v. Superior Court (2003) 31 Cal.4th 1026 (CourtListener text)
citations.quote: We reiterate the limits of our holding. An employer continues to be strictly liable for hostile environment sexual harassment by a supervisor. An employee’s failure to report harassment to the employer is not a defense on the merits to the employee’s action under the FEHA, but at most it serves to reduce the damages recoverable.

The quotations below are the two provisions that most directly fix those boundaries — the coworker sentence of subdivision (j)(1), which by its own terms governs harassment “by an employee, other than an agent or supervisor,” and the court’s statement of the limits of its holding. No source cited in this document states how the FEHA interacts with any other statute, and nothing in this document evaluates any particular set of facts or tells any reader what to do.
